extracted.intended_audience: readers, students, and aspiring literary critics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for how to read and understand great literature: close, word-by-word reading that seeks the author's thought and passion, combined with cultivated sensitivity and disciplined feeling; also cultural injunctions to value books, science, art, nature, and compassion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Close, word-by-word examination
rubrics_metrics.description: Watch every accent and expression, and put yourself always in the author’s place; practise a 'word-by-word examination' of your author which is rightly called 'reading.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘Watching every accent and expression, and putting ourselves always in the author’s place, annihilating our own personality, and seeking to enter into his, so as to be able assuredly to say, “Thus Milton thought.”’ Example: detailed parsing of Milton's pictorial choices (mitred locks, keys, 'creep, intrude, climb'). Close reading is the method by which one extracts meaning from lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid projecting your own meaning; seek authorial thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not read texts by putting your own meaning into their words; aim to discover 'Thus [the author] thought,' not 'Thus I thought.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Great men do not play stage tricks with doctrines; therefore the reader must resist the temptation to eye texts askance or whisper them under the breath. The reader must honestly attempt to understand the text on its own terms rather than impose personal prejudices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humility about interpretive limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Accept that with greater authors you cannot quickly or fully fathom their meaning; much of great literature resists immediate capture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton, Shakespeare, Dante — their meanings are wide and often unfathomable in full; a little honest study will reveal some things, but you must be content with partial understanding and continual learning rather than confident pronouncements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear away prejudice before study ('break up your fallow ground')
rubrics_metrics.description: First burn away your own rough, entangled prejudices and careless notions — 'break up your fallow ground, and sow not among thorns.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reader must 'annihilate our own personality' and 'set fire' to the 'jungle' of preconception so that true literary work can begin. This is an ethical and intellectual cleansing: do not let chance prejudice masquerade as judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enter into the author’s heart: cultivate disciplined passion (sensation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reading must not be merely intellectual; one must 'enter into their Hearts' and share their just and mighty passion. Sensation (passion) is essential and ennobling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues for more, not less, sensation: sensitivity is the measure of humanity. But sensation must be disciplined and tested — not the first wild passion, but a noble, just, and enduring feeling grown by study and discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop 'tact' or touch-faculty (fineness of sensation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultivate a fine and full sensation — the 'tact' or 'touch-faculty' — which enables quick understanding, sympathy, and nuanced perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vulgarity is essentially a want of sensation (callousness). The fine reader/writer resembles the Mimosa or 'the pure woman' in possessing acute sensibility; this sensibility sanctifies reason and permits recognition of what is good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discipline passions; test feelings for justice and force
rubrics_metrics.description: True passion is disciplined and tested; the first passions are often vain, false, and treacherous and must be controlled so feeling is both forceful and just.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate mean curiosity or selfish sensation (prurient interest in trivial tales) from noble curiosity (questioning about great truths). The reader should cultivate passions that are measured, continuous, and just.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain just, measured, and continuous feeling (not mob sentiment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim for constancy and justice in feeling rather than volatile, crowd-driven emotions; a gentleman's feelings should be measured and continuous rather than mob-like infection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mob 'thinks by infection' and can be teased into any opinion; the cultivated reader resists being led by ephemeral fits of feeling and seeks sustained, reasoned moral response to literature and events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commit to books: buy, read, re-read, and annotate
rubrics_metrics.description: Value books materially and intellectually: if a book is worth reading it is worth buying; read and re-read, love, and mark books so they become a usable store of thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Books are described as 'bread of flour' and 'sweet as honey'; cheapness and casual borrowing diminish their perceived worth. Practical guidance: acquire books, reread them, mark passages for later reference as one would keep weapons in an armoury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value and support science
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not merely profit from scientific advances; a cultured nation (and reader) must actively value and support scientific work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: failure to purchase the Solenhofen fossil collection for the nation is reproached. The reader should recognize and honour scientific endeavour rather than treating discoveries as incidental shop-goods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value art for its own sake, not merely as market commodity
rubrics_metrics.description: Love and preserve art beyond its marketplace value; do not treat pictures merely like bills pasted on walls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique of national indifference to true care for pictures and historic works; readers and literary practitioners should learn to see and respect art, not merely use it as a commodity or status symbol.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value nature; resist vulgar tourism and destruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Respect the deep and sacred sensations produced by natural scenery; avoid turning places of wonder into vulgar playgrounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: railway-bridges over falls, noisy, destructive tourism. The cultivated reader/writer preserves reverence for nature as a source of true feeling and imagination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate and practise compassion
rubrics_metrics.description: Compassion is an essential moral and literary capacity; do not despise compassion or become callous to human suffering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The coroner's case of Michael Collins is given as a moral lesson: true readers and writers should be moved to pity and moral action by accounts of human need rather than shrugging them off.
